How to get your song on the radioStep by step

By the RadioReach team Updated August 18, 2026 3 min read Core guides

On this page
  • Step 1: Pick realistic targets
  • Step 2: Verify each station's submission policy
  • Step 3: Find the right human
  • Step 4: Prepare your assets before you pitch
  • Step 5: Write a short, personalized pitch
  • Step 6: Send in waves and track everything
  • Step 7: Follow up once, politely
  • Step 8: Turn spins into momentum

Getting airplay as an independent artist is not a mystery or a lottery — it is a process. Stations need a steady supply of new music, and the programmers who choose it are reachable. What separates artists who get played from artists who get ignored is rarely the music alone: it is targeting, preparation, and follow-through. This guide walks through the whole sequence, step by step.

Step 1: Pick realistic targets

Radio is not one thing. A college station with a volunteer music director, a community station with genre shows, a noncommercial music station, and a commercial Top 40 outlet have completely different rules about where music comes from. Commercial radio rarely accepts unsolicited material; its playlists flow through labels, distributors, and professional promoters.

Your first campaigns belong where independent music is structurally welcome:

  • College and university stations
  • Community and noncommercial music stations
  • Internet radio and online genre shows
  • Specialty programs on larger stations that spotlight local or new music

Start with stations whose playlists already contain artists who sound like you. If you cannot name two, research more before pitching — this single filter predicts results more than anything else in the process.

Step 2: Verify each station's submission policy

Many stations publish exactly how they want music submitted — an address, a form, a set of rules. Find it and follow it precisely. Programming staff triage on process: a submission that ignores stated rules is the easiest one to delete.

Where no policy exists, a short personalized email to the right person is the universal fallback. If a station clearly states it does not accept unsolicited music, believe it and move on.

Step 3: Find the right human

The fastest no is a yes sent to the wrong person. Before pitching, identify who actually programs music like yours at that station:

  • Music director (MD) — screens and adds new releases at most college and community stations
  • Program director (PD) — oversees the schedule and often the sound
  • Genre director — programs a specific category like hip-hop, loud rock, electronic, or jazz
  • Specialty-show host — the decision-maker for a single show that fits your sound

Contacts churn constantly in radio, especially at student-run stations. Verify names and roles each campaign — our glossary covers these titles and how stations use them.

Step 4: Prepare your assets before you pitch

Interest dies fast when the follow-up materials are not ready. Assemble once, reuse everywhere:

  • One streaming link that works without login friction
  • A clean radio edit if the original contains profanity — broadcast rules are strict
  • A one-sheet: a single page with artwork, track info, a two-line bio, contact, and the link
  • A short EPK or press page for programmers who want more

Our EPK and one-sheet guide shows exactly what radio programmers want in each.

Step 5: Write a short, personalized pitch

The pitch that gets answered is under 150 words and clearly built for one station: who you are, what the release is, one honest sentence on why it fits this station or show, and the streaming link. No attachments. No press-release formatting. No "guaranteed hit."

You do not need to write every email from scratch — use a tested pitch template and swap in the personalized line each time.

Step 6: Send in waves and track everything

Send in batches of 20–40 stations so replies, questions, and link requests get answered while they are warm. Keep a simple log — station, contact, date sent, response — so you never pitch the same person twice and you can see patterns in who replies.

Step 7: Follow up once, politely

Programmers lose emails constantly; one nudge is expected professional behavior. After seven to ten days, reply to your own message with one or two sentences. Anything beyond that spends goodwill you will want for your next release.

Step 8: Turn spins into momentum

Watch station playlists and college/community charts for your name each week. When a station plays you:

  • Thank the programmer — briefly and like a human
  • Share the spin publicly and tag the station
  • Add the confirmation to your one-sheet: "currently spinning on [station]"
  • Lead with it in the next wave of pitches

Airplay compounds. Stations are more likely to add an artist other stations are already playing, and each confirmed spin makes the next pitch easier to believe.

Frequently asked questions

Can an unknown artist really get radio play?

Yes — in the parts of the dial where programmers choose music themselves. College, community, noncommercial, and internet stations add independent releases every week. What is unrealistic for a new unknown artist is commercial chart radio, which is driven by label pipelines and monitored promotion.

How much does it cost to get a song on the radio?

Doing it yourself costs time, not money: research, pitching, and follow-up. Hiring an independent radio promoter for a single campaign typically runs from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. Our comparison guide breaks down when paying is worth it.

Do I need a professional recording?

Your song needs to sound competitive next to what the station already plays. That does not require a major-label budget, but a poorly mixed master will not survive programming. If you would not pitch it to a playlist curator, do not pitch it to radio.

How many stations should I expect to play me?

Response rates are modest for every artist and promoter. Plan for a small percentage of stations adding your track, and treat each confirmed spin as evidence for the next campaign rather than a disappointment against the total.
